implementation_notes: The pattern is absorbed into the language: `Array.prototype.filter` is a built-in method whose callback is the criterion, and messages that fail it are simply absent from the returned array, so there is no filter object to design. For push-style feeds (EventEmitter, WebSocket, worker messages) the same predicate becomes a guard in the listener or a `Transform` stream that drops chunks, and in reactive code the `filter` operator on an observable plays the identical role. A named predicate function is the idiomatic container for a reusable criterion; a filter class is not.
pitfalls: filter() copies the accepted elements into a new array; on a hot feed it is cheaper to guard inside a loop than to build a filtered copy per batch.
The callback receives (value, index, array): a predicate that accepts a second parameter silently gets the index, which usually breaks the criterion.
A dropped message is gone; without a counter or a dead-letter path an over-strict predicate is indistinguishable from an idle queue.

variants.name: Lazy iterator helper (Iterator.prototype.filter)
variants.idiom_name: Iterator.prototype.filter / for...of over an iterator helper
variants.implementation_notes: With iterator helpers, `it.filter(pred)` returns a lazy iterator helper that yields matching values on demand; unlike the array method it neither copies nor needs the whole feed, so it composes with generators and unbounded sources and works in `for...of` (breaking out stops pulling upstream). The trade-offs are single consumption and the loss of indexing and length; use it for streaming message sources, and keep Array.prototype.filter for materialised batches. Async sources need async iterator helpers or an in-loop guard inside `for await`.
pitfalls: An iterator helper is consumed once: iterating it a second time yields nothing.
There is no index and no length; converting back with Array.from re-materialises the whole feed and loses the laziness that motivated the helper.
Applying the synchronous helper to an async iterable yields promises instead of messages; async sources need `for await` plus an explicit guard.
